summary: Review-required audit trail for the live DNS cache flush card. The app already exposes the command-backed action and repo docs point to the same ipconfig flow, but the card has not yet been promoted through the validated research-provider pipeline.

setting.name: Flush DNS Cache
setting.casual_explanation: This clears the Windows DNS resolver cache so the next lookups are fetched fresh instead of reusing cached records.
setting.why_people_change_it: People use it when diagnosing name-resolution issues or when they want the system to stop using stale cached DNS answers.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: This is a one-shot repair action rather than a persistent setting. It is useful for troubleshooting, but there is nothing durable to roll back after the cache has been flushed.
setting.professional_notes: The live app models this card as a command tweak that detects by reading ipconfig /displaydns and applies by running ipconfig /flushdns. Repo network docs and tweak provenance both map the tweak id to that same command-backed action. The record stays review-required until command-backed maintenance actions are promoted into the validated research-provider surface.

decision.why: The current ipconfig-based action is clear and documented in repo sources, but the card still lives outside the validated research-provider surface and has no rollback state.
blocking_issues: The card still ships only as a first-party network utility and has not been promoted into the research-provider surface.
This is a one-shot troubleshooting action without rollback.
decision.promotion_disposition_reason: Closed as rejected for research-provider promotion because the live action is one-shot, destructive, high-risk, reboot-sensitive, or lacks a rollback story suitable for a validated tweak card.
decision.promotion_reopen_criteria: Reopen only if the app gains a verified rollback/snapshot contract and dedicated validation proof for the exact action.

open_questions: Do we want one-shot repair actions like DNS cache flush to live in the long-term research corpus, or should they stay app-only by policy?
If promoted later, should these command utilities live in a dedicated repair/maintenance surface instead of the normal research card lane?
